Introduction/AI-SDLC/Product discovery

Development guide

Product discovery

Research the problem, identify worthwhile opportunities, validate concepts and hand over the evidence for a bounded implementation. Business value and technical feasibility shape the decision together, from the first investigation through to delivery.

Use AI to organise research, challenge assumptions and explore options within a shared Product, Design and Engineering team. Check generated claims against user evidence and executable technical results, then carry the findings and remaining uncertainty into implementation. This guidance applies when AI assists discovery, whether or not the product itself contains AI.

Status: Draft working guidance · Last reviewed: 28 October 2026

On this page

Purpose and entry criteria

Product discovery reduces uncertainty about which problem to solve, which concept to pursue and whether the team can deliver and operate it. Ideation generates options within discovery. Research, opportunity identification, concept validation and validation handover connect those options to evidence and an investment decision.

Business discovery examines user needs, organisational value, adoption and viability. Technical discovery examines capabilities, data, architecture, integration, security, operating conditions and delivery constraints. Product, Design and Engineering work on both together: technical findings can reveal an opportunity or rule out a promising concept.

Start or reopen discovery when the decision is uncertain

Enter with a user problem, strategic objective, operational risk, obligation or newly available capability. Reopen discovery when research, technical spikes, implementation or production results challenge the expected value, intended behaviour or feasibility. A well-understood defect can enter implementation directly with a bounded issue and acceptance criteria.

  • Decision and scope: name what the team needs to learn, the affected users and systems, exclusions and the next investment decision.
  • Initial context: bring existing research, service measures, alternatives, architecture and known dependencies; mark assumptions and access gaps.
  • People and access: name Product, Design and Engineering contributors, the decision owner and relevant service or data owners. Arrange permitted access to users, evidence and technical environments.
  • Learning budget: agree a time and cost limit, review point and stop conditions proportionate to the uncertainty and consequences.

The outcome is a justified next decision: investigate further, implement a bounded scope, change direction, defer or stop. See the relationship between discovery and implementation.

Working guidance

The stages and checks below are recommended working practices, mapped to local roles and decision authority. Scale the depth to the decision; they do not establish new EDS approval gates.

Four connected discovery stages

Use these stages to organise the work and its evidence. They overlap and repeat: begin a feasibility spike as soon as a critical technical assumption appears, and return to research when a concept fails for an unexpected reason. Carry business and technical questions through every stage.

Evidence and decisions across discovery
StageBusiness and user questionsTechnical questionsOutput and next decision
1 ResearchBusiness and user questionsWho experiences the problem, why, and at what cost?Technical questionsWhat exists, what can be reused and which constraints need investigation?Output and next decisionResearch synthesis, baselines and assumptions; identify credible opportunities.
2 Identify opportunitiesBusiness and user questionsWhich problem and outcome justify attention?Technical questionsWhich capabilities enable an option, and which dependencies could prevent it?Output and next decisionPrioritised opportunities and concept briefs; choose the next experiments.
3 Validate conceptsBusiness and user questionsDoes the concept improve the task and fit the organisation?Technical questionsCan the critical path work within the agreed quality, cost and delivery limits?Output and next decisionLinked experiment and feasibility results; proceed, rework, defer or stop.
4 Validation handoverBusiness and user questionsWhat bounded outcome and behaviour does the evidence support?Technical questionsWhich approach is feasible, under what conditions, and what still needs proving?Output and next decisionVersioned requirements, evidence and owned unknowns; agree readiness for the next investment.

Choose frameworks for the discovery question

A framework organises discovery work; a method gathers evidence about a particular question. Use the four stages above as the shared process, and choose frameworks within them. Product School’s discovery guide [8] introduces six useful approaches: dual-track discovery and delivery, Jobs To Be Done, Double Diamond, Design Sprint, Lean Startup and Opportunity Solution Trees.

The table shows where each approach helps and the working artefact to retain. The technical checks are this guide’s recommendations: no framework removes the need to investigate feasibility or review the evidence.

Combine only the practices the decision needs

For example, use JTBD interviews to understand a task, an Opportunity Solution Tree to compare responses, and a focused sprint to test an interaction. Use Build–Measure–Learn to repeat the experiments and continuous discovery to keep learning connected to delivery. Record the question, evidence and next decision rather than treating framework completion as progress.

Work as one product team with agents

Product definition, design, engineering and assurance need a shared view of the evidence. Keep the people making these judgements involved throughout discovery, with agents supporting work in the same product context.

Keep AI assistance connected to evidence

Give each AI-assisted task a question, permitted inputs, an expected output and a human reviewer. Distinguish source observations, model interpretations and untested suggestions in the shared record. Ask for traceable references; check that the cited material exists and supports the claim before it changes a decision.

Practice inspiration: Product School’s AI discovery guide [17]. The checks throughout this chapter are recommended applications. NIST’s Generative AI Profile [19], action MS-2.5-003 and Appendix A.1.6, support checking generated citations and retaining content provenance.

Bring Product, Design and Engineering together

Sumit Sheth’s “3-in-a-Box” model brings Product, Design and Engineering together around intent, interaction and implementation. Any discipline can initiate discovery; the three shape and test the experience together. Apply this as a collaboration pattern, mapped to local roles.

Use the concept brief to align on the outcome, intended interaction and feasibility. Name the people covering each discipline, then link the brief to the experiment record and next decision.

Source: [5] on continuous co-creation and the three disciplines.

Make collaboration part of each discovery stage

Product and research contributors lead investigation of needs and value; Design leads experience and inclusion; Engineering leads feasibility and technical options. Work together on research, opportunity selection, experiments and handover. Choose the riskiest assumption and review the same observations and technical results. Revise the behaviour, technical approach and PRD in the same learning cycle. Involve QA, research, operations, data, security and risk specialists where the uncertainty calls for their expertise.

Shared ownership of the outcome still needs named decision owners. Record disagreements and escalate unresolved scope, investment or risk choices to the authorised person. The triad does not replace specialist assurance or approval.

Use the table to agree responsibilities and decision owners across the team. One person may cover several disciplines.

Human judgement and agent-supported work
ParticipantHuman judgement and accountabilityAgent-supported work
ProductProblem, outcomes, priorities, trade-offs and thesisResearch summaries, options, draft specifications and decision evidence
DesignUser behaviour, desirability, usability and interaction principlesConcept variants, prototypes, journey analysis and heuristic checks
Engineering and architectureFeasibility, architecture, reversibility, security and operational qualityCode exploration, technical spikes, plans, tests and dependency analysis
AI and dataData quality, model behaviour, evaluation design and runtime controlsDataset analysis, evaluations, tracing and model comparison
Risk and compliancePolicy interpretation, thresholds, exceptions and accountable acceptanceContinuous checks, evidence collection, control mapping and risk screening
AgentsNo organisational accountabilityResearch, challenge, specification drafting, prototyping, testing and evaluation

For this to work, the shared environment needs:

  • access to current, relevant product and technical context;
  • clear ownership, permissions and decision authority;
  • visible agent activity, sources, outputs and status;
  • a structured route for review, feedback and exceptions; and
  • explicit human approval for high-consequence decisions.

Delegating work does not delegate accountability. The exchange also runs both ways: technical feasibility should shape ideas early, and user and business intent should shape architecture early. Doing both reduces late surprises about security, data location, performance, model limitations and operations.

Next step: bring Product, Design and Engineering to the next experiment. Agree the outcome, interaction and feasibility question, then review the prototype and evidence together. Read about human–agent team composition.

Source: [1] “Structure the team right”.

1 Research the problem and technical context

Begin with a research plan that connects each uncertainty to a method, evidence source, owner and decision. Combine observation and interviews with service data and technical investigation. Interview users who struggle or use workarounds as well as willing early adopters, covering relevant access needs and operational roles.

Build a shared evidence base

Research coverage and working artefacts
AreaInvestigationWorking evidence
Users and the whole journeyInvestigationObserve real tasks across roles, channels and systems. Explore unmet needs, exclusion, workarounds and current alternatives.Working evidenceSource-linked observations, journey map, user groups and research gaps.
Business and service contextInvestigationExamine intended outcomes, demand, current cost, policy intent, existing commitments and adoption barriers. Include operating and change costs.Working evidenceBaseline measures, value hypothesis, stakeholder map and constraints.
Technology and operationsInvestigationInspect relevant code, architecture, interfaces, incidents and runtime behaviour with system owners. Compare existing services and reusable capabilities.Working evidenceSystem and data-flow map, dependency owners, reuse options and technical unknowns.
Market and enabling capabilitiesInvestigationReview comparable services, suppliers and new capabilities against the problem. Check availability and claims with their owners or primary sources.Working evidenceAlternatives, capability findings and assumptions requiring direct tests.

Separate observations, interpretations and assumptions. Keep source, date, affected population and limitations beside each finding. An analytics trend can reveal where to investigate; interviews can explain a difficulty. Neither alone establishes that a proposed solution will cause the intended improvement.

Use AI synthesis to direct the next investigation

Keep feedback themes current and use interview excerpts to direct review. Retain the source passage or timestamp, collection date, user group and supporting and contradictory observations. A reviewer checks the surrounding context before accepting an interpretation; a transcript alone may miss behaviour visible in the recording or direct observation.

Count distinct participants or events after removing duplicates. Compare equivalent periods and channels before calling a theme a trend; record changes in who supplied the data. Preserve rare but consequential issues, and check an independently selected sample of source records for findings the clustering omitted.

At evidence reviews, choose the next question from verified changes, rather than sentiment rank alone. Name the next user study or technical test and its owner. Set the review cadence to incoming evidence and decision urgency. Confirm generated technical explanations with system owners, current documentation or executable checks.

Investigate feasibility from the start

Engineering should lead technical investigation alongside user and business research. Record the enabling options as well as the constraints. Distinguish constraints the team can change from dependencies controlled elsewhere, and confirm access, ownership and lead times before treating them as available.

Technical discovery questions and feasibility evidence
AreaQuestions to investigateEvidence to retain
Architecture and reuseQuestions to investigateCan an existing service, platform or supplier meet the need? What changes to the current system would be required?Evidence to retainOptions and trade-offs, affected boundaries, reuse checks and an outline of the critical path.
Data and integrationQuestions to investigateIs the necessary data accessible, suitable and permitted for this use? Do interfaces, identity, contracts and quotas support the journey?Evidence to retainData samples and quality findings, interface checks, dependency confirmations and access gaps.
Quality and operating conditionsQuestions to investigateWhich latency, volume, availability, accessibility and recovery limits matter? Who can support and operate the capability?Evidence to retainMeasured baselines, agreed test conditions, operational input and measurable quality targets.
Security and privacyQuestions to investigateWhat data and actions cross trust boundaries? Which controls, permissions and specialist decisions affect the concept?Evidence to retainInitial threat and data-flow notes, control constraints and unresolved decisions with owners.
Delivery and lifetime costQuestions to investigateDo the skills, capacity, procurement, migration and external lead times fit the next scope? What are the build, run, support and exit costs?Evidence to retainEffort and cost ranges with assumptions, dependencies, migration options and uncertainty.
AI capability when relevantQuestions to investigateDoes an AI approach outperform a simpler alternative on representative cases? Are quality, latency, cost, data use and human fallback acceptable?Evidence to retainModel and data versions, evaluation cases, failure analysis, baseline comparison and cost per successful task.

Use a time-limited technical spike when inspection cannot resolve an important assumption. State the question, test conditions, pass and failure limits, budget and owner before starting. Exercise the critical integration or capability, retain results and code references, then state which options remain feasible. A successful mock does not establish that the real dependency will work.

Discovery establishes enough confidence to choose the next scope. Detailed technical design develops in the technical requirements document (TRD) during implementation. Record early architecture decisions and constraints so delivery can challenge or refine them without repeating the investigation.

Review whether the evidence can support opportunity selection

Product, Design and Engineering review the research synthesis together. Move forward when it identifies a credible problem or enabling opportunity, a baseline or plan to establish one, relevant constraints and the most consequential unknowns. Return to targeted research when contradictory findings or missing access could change that choice.

Reference: [6] GOV.UK discovery guidance covers users, context, constraints and alternatives. This guide uses discovery more broadly to include concept testing; GOV.UK separates that work into alpha. The technical questions above are recommended working checks.

2 Identify and prioritise opportunities

An opportunity is an evidence-backed problem or potential outcome worth pursuing. A concept is one possible response. Keep them separate so the team can reject a solution without losing the underlying need.

Turn research into an opportunity shortlist

  1. Group findings by need and cause. Trace each opportunity to affected users, the task, observed friction or foreseeable risk, and its consequence. Identify where a change could improve the outcome.
  2. Write an opportunity record. Capture evidence and confidence, baseline, expected value, strategic fit, urgency, enabling capabilities, dependencies and the highest-risk assumptions.
  3. Compare opportunities jointly. Product, Design and Engineering weigh reach, severity, frequency, inclusion, expected benefit, feasibility, lifetime cost and dependency risk. Record uncertainty and the reason for the ranking.
  4. Choose the next learning investment. Select opportunities to investigate or validate, record deferred and rejected ones with reasons, and assign an owner and review trigger. A high-value but uncertain opportunity can justify a small feasibility experiment.

Use scores to make assumptions visible, rather than to manufacture precision. Keep mandatory obligations and intolerable risks explicit when they override discretionary priorities. Revisit the shortlist when new capabilities, constraints or evidence change the available choices.

Example · connect an outcome to tests

Outcome: reduce incomplete access requests. Opportunity: staff cannot identify which information each request needs. Concepts: clearer guidance, a guided form or a draft-request assistant. Assumption tests: compare task completion and correction effort; separately test whether the identity service exposes the permitted attributes. A failed integration test changes the concept choice without removing the underlying user need.

Challenge priorities with evidence and alternative plans

Use delivery history and competitor research to propose questions about missed needs. Check planned investment against actual effort, measured outcomes, obligations and dependencies before describing the pattern as strategic drift. A launch announcement shows a supplier’s offer; any inferred customer need remains a hypothesis for research.

Compare an earlier-delivery scenario with one that resolves uncertainty sooner. Give both the same outcomes, resource assumptions and constraints. Engineering checks dependency lead times, reversibility, quality targets and operating cost. Record which additional evidence could change the sequence, then agree one bounded next investment.

Keep the assumptions behind any generated ranking visible. Test whether plausible changes in benefit, effort or dependency estimates change the ordering. A model’s confidence or agreement across generated answers does not supply the missing evidence.

State a thesis that can be disproved

A product thesis is a claim about why a product or capability should exist, written so that evidence could show it to be wrong. Without that property, each prototype tends to refine the idea rather than test it.

Recognise where the idea came from

An idea usually starts from a user or business problem, or from a new technical capability. Neither starting point is better, but each fails in its own way. Both need to arrive at an opportunity that is valuable, feasible and supported by evidence.

Two starting points for a product idea
Starting pointStrengthCommon failureQuestion to ask
Problem pull: a user or business problemAnchored in real demand and outcomesIncremental thinking that assumes today’s workflow must remainCould the problem be removed, rather than today’s solution improved?
Technology push: a new capability or lower costReveals options that were previously impossibleAn impressive capability searching for a valuable problemWhat meaningful problem is now feasible to solve for the first time?

Write a short concept brief

Before committing to scope, dates or estimates, capture the thesis in a short concept brief. Aim for one page, with links to supporting evidence. Any discipline can draft it; Product, Design and Engineering refine it together.

The following is a suggested working format. Record:

  • User, problem and evidence: the target user, their task, the consequence of doing nothing, and linked observations, requests or analysis. Distinguish a request from evidence of its underlying need.
  • Outcome and value: the outcome the user needs, the value to the organisation and why the opportunity matters now.
  • Proposed direction and alternatives: the initial solution hypothesis, the expected interaction and the alternatives worth comparing.
  • Feasibility and boundaries: enabling capabilities, known constraints, exclusions, risks, dependencies and unresolved assumptions.
  • Falsification criteria: evidence or limits, agreed in advance, that would trigger a redesign, a pivot or a stop.

Name the brief’s owner, next experiment and decision owner. Share it with relevant stakeholders before seeking the next investment, then update it as evidence changes. Develop the PRD from this brief as the intended behaviour becomes clearer.

Example · fictional thesis

A squad believes that service desk staff will resolve routine access requests faster with an assistant that drafts responses from the knowledge base. The thesis is weakened if staff cannot complete the task correctly, or if checking and correcting drafts removes the expected time saving. The experiment below turns those concerns into a test and a decision rule.

Test the problem statement before the solution

The Defence Product Playbook traces most weak products to a weak problem statement. It suggests building the statement from six questions, the 6W: what goes wrong, where, when and how often, who feels it, why it happens and why it matters. Then check what you have written against four criteria, the 4C.

The 4C problem-statement check, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
CriterionWhat the statement shows
ClarityOne user group, the task they attempt, the friction, and how severe and frequent it is
ConsequenceThe quantified cost if the problem stays unsolved
CauseA theory of change: the causal chain and the step worth intervening at
ConfirmationEvidence that supports the identified cause

The playbook names four traps: an aspiration, a solution in disguise, an end-of-life notice and a vague pain. An end-of-life notice alone does not explain the consequence. Describe the current or foreseeable effects on support, security maintenance, compatibility, recoverability and mission continuity, with relevant dates and evidence. Teams can act before a user-facing failure: for example, plan migration before vendor security support ends or recovery becomes unviable.

For discretionary improvements, severity, frequency and reach (SFR) can help compare problem statements when there are more opportunities than teams. Score each dimension low, medium or high, record the evidence and uncertainty, and use the scores to support judgement rather than as an automatic ranking.

Apply explicit overrides for mandatory obligations and intolerable risks. A rare problem affecting few people may still warrant priority because of mission failure, serious harm, security exposure or an accessibility barrier. Record the consequence, applicable obligation or risk threshold, urgency and decision owner before comparing discretionary opportunities.

Next step: for your shortlisted opportunity, write one sentence each for the user, the outcome and the assumption that would most damage the case if it were false. Then agree the evidence that would show it is false, and check the problem statement against the 4C.

Source: [1] “Define the problem, measure the value”.

Explore alternative concepts before choosing one

The Design Council’s Double Diamond separates widening the options from narrowing them. The first diamond explores and then defines the problem; the second develops possible solutions and then tests them at small scale, rejecting those that do not work.

How this maps to discovery: Research widens understanding of the problem; opportunity identification narrows the choice. Concept exploration opens the solution space; validation tests the options. These are repeated learning activities, not a separate lifecycle or a production release decision.

The first diamond covers the problem space: discover widens understanding, define narrows it to a chosen problem. The second covers the solution space: develop widens the options, deliver narrows them through testing. The blue points mark decisions in this guide’s adaptation.

The Defence Product Playbook uses the same lens. It places problem definition in the first diamond and testing in the second, where testing has the greatest effect.

Compare materially different concepts, including process or content changes, reuse, purchase, partnership and building a new capability. Include doing nothing as a baseline. Engineering assesses the enabling approach and likely costs for each; avoid choosing a concept solely because its prototype is easy to generate.

Use AI differently when widening and narrowing

  • When widening, use AI to research broadly, summarise evidence, generate different concepts, surface hidden assumptions and explore alternative journeys or technical approaches.
  • When narrowing, compare options against user value, strength of evidence, feasibility, cost, risk and strategic fit. Do not choose an option because it is the most polished or the easiest to generate.

Use persona simulations only to rehearse questions or propose cases to investigate. Label them as generated assumptions and keep them outside participant counts, quotations and outcome measures. Research with the affected users still supplies the evidence. Nielsen Norman Group’s evaluation [18] supports this distinction; it does not establish how every future model will perform.

Challenge the proposal before refining it

AI can turn a stakeholder request into a polished specification quickly. That speed creates a risk: refining an idea nobody has challenged. Before commitment, ask a reviewer, or an agent instructed to act as a critic, to work through these questions:

  1. What evidence shows that the problem is important and severe enough?
  2. What happens if the organisation does nothing?
  3. Which users experience the problem, and which do not?
  4. Why this solution rather than a materially different one?
  5. Which assumption could invalidate the whole thesis?
  6. What is the cheapest credible experiment that could disprove it?
  7. Which requirements conflict, and what fails at much greater scale?

When AI proposes an objection, ask which assumption it challenges and which observation or executable test could resolve it. Include unavailable data, unsupported permissions, integration limits and operating cost. Have a reviewer examine the evidence independently of the proposal’s generated defence; a second answer from the same model is not independent corroboration.

This challenge complements user research and domain expertise; it does not replace them. Regulated, safety-critical, legally consequential and highly specialised questions still need qualified human reviewers.

Next step: before the next refinement session, put the seven questions to someone who was not involved in shaping the idea. Record the answers the team cannot yet support with evidence.

Sources: [2]; [1] “Test early, iterate fast”.

3 Validate concepts and feasibility

Choose the riskiest assumption across value, usability, technical feasibility and business viability. Run user tests and technical experiments in the same learning cycle, allowing each to change the concept. A desirable experience with an unworkable integration, or an affordable technical solution that users cannot use, needs further discovery.

Complementary evidence for concept validation
RiskQuestionEvidence and limits
ValueQuestionDoes this solve a problem users need addressed?Evidence and limitsObserved behaviour, task outcomes or a bounded pilot compared with the current approach; stated enthusiasm alone is weak evidence.
Usability and inclusionQuestionCan relevant users complete the journey?Evidence and limitsTask-based testing of critical states, including accessibility, permissions, interruptions and recovery.
Technical feasibilityQuestionCan we build, integrate and operate it within the agreed constraints?Evidence and limitsExecutable spikes on the critical path, representative data, measured quality and cost, and confirmed dependencies. Record differences from production.
Business viabilityQuestionCan the organisation sustain and adopt it?Evidence and limitsBenefit and lifetime cost ranges, operational capacity, change and procurement constraints, and input from accountable specialists.

Risk framing: [3] SVPG, The Four Big Risks. The suggested evidence and checks are this guide’s application.

Prototype the uncertainty that could change the decision

Choose a prototype by the uncertainty it needs to resolve. A sketch may be enough to test a journey; a working integration may be needed to test feasibility. AI can help produce either, but speed and visual polish do not establish useful evidence.

Check experiment safety before prototyping

Before creating or running a prototype, the experiment owner records the following checks with the relevant data, security and research specialists. Resolve unclear permissions or use a safer experiment design before proceeding.

  • Permitted data: identify what may be collected, entered into AI tools, stored and shared. Use synthetic or appropriately de-identified data where possible; record retention and deletion arrangements.
  • Approved tools: confirm that the tools, models and hosting are approved for the intended data and use, including how providers handle submitted information.
  • Participant information: explain the purpose, prototype limitations, AI involvement, what will be recorded and how findings will be used. Confirm consent or other applicable participation requirements and a way to withdraw or report concerns.
  • Access restrictions: define who can use the prototype, access its data or invoke connected systems. Isolate the experiment, limit permissions and agree stop conditions for unexpected effects.
  • Prototype disposition: name the owner and expiry date, and decide how code, data and credentials will be deleted, archived or reviewed for reuse. Any promotion to production follows the applicable implementation and release checks.

Choose the experiment by the evidence needed

Use an experiment to test an explicit assumption and inform a decision. Interviews and co-creation can expose needs and possible responses; QA checks implementation behaviour. When testing whether a change caused an outcome, plan a credible comparison and account for other explanations. Keep these purposes visible when choosing a method.

Product School’s experimentation playbook [9] covers split tests, multivariate tests, demand probes, landing pages, usability prototypes, manual simulations, staged rollouts and adaptive personalisation. The catalogue below adds technical and operational tests, with recommended evidence limits for each.

Experiment catalogue for business and technical discovery
MethodQuestion and signalLimits and technical follow-up
Fake-door or smoke testQuestion and signalDoes an early-access offer attract interest? Compare eligible exposures with selections or requests to participate.Limits and technical follow-upExplain availability when users select the offer. Interest does not establish sustained value, willingness to pay or build feasibility. Avoid implying that a consequential action has completed.
Landing page or message testQuestion and signalWhich value proposition attracts the intended audience? Record qualified visits, enquiries and sign-ups.Limits and technical follow-upRecord the audience and acquisition channel. Recruitment bias or different traffic can explain changes; use controlled allocation when claiming one message outperforms another.
Prototype and task-based usability testQuestion and signalCan users complete the intended task? Observe comprehension, errors, completion, assistance and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upA small qualitative study can reveal friction, but cannot estimate population-wide uplift. Note simulated behaviour and untested access needs.
Concierge testQuestion and signalDoes a service help when people deliver it openly? Observe outcomes, repeat use and the effort required to provide support.Limits and technical follow-upRecord manual effort and cost. Treat this as a test of service value; separately establish whether automation can reproduce the useful result.
Wizard of Oz test
Method guidance [14]		Question and signalHow do users interact with an apparently automated interface whose responses are supplied by a person? Observe expectations and task behaviour.Limits and technical follow-upAgree the participant briefing and debriefing in the research plan. Keep operator responses within plausible system limits; a skilled human’s output does not validate a model or integration.
Technical spike or proof of conceptQuestion and signalCan a critical capability or integration work under specified conditions? Run an executable check and measure the relevant limits.Limits and technical follow-upTest the real dependency where permitted. Record mocks, environment differences, test data, versions, failure cases and reproducible results. It does not establish demand.

Multivariate test
Method guidance [16]		Question and signalWhich combination of factors works, and do they interact? Compare planned combinations, such as content and layout variants.Limits and technical follow-upPlan enough observations for the combinations. Observe reliability, task outcomes, support demand and recovery.Limits and technical follow-upApply the release checks and stop criteria. Rollout monitoring alone is not a causal comparison. Keep an explicit control design when testing an improvement claim.
Adaptive personalisationQuestion and signalDoes a changing allocation policy improve outcomes across relevant users? Evaluate the policy and important segments over time.Limits and technical follow-upUse a comparison and analysis suited to adaptive allocation, with specialist input. Set exploration limits and guardrails; automatic adaptation alone does not demonstrate benefit.

The catalogue is working guidance for this lifecycle. [14] explains human-controlled prototypes; [15] supports controlled-test design; [16] explains multivariate combinations. Technical spikes and AI evaluations extend the earlier feasibility guidance.

Choose a method proportionate to uncertainty and exposure

  • Need or demand unclear: start with research and a demand probe. Use the resulting signal to choose a deeper value test.
  • Journey unclear: use task-based prototypes, a concierge service or a Wizard of Oz study. Pair simulated capabilities with a technical check.
  • Critical dependency unclear: start the technical spike early. A positive usability result cannot resolve unavailable data or an incompatible interface.
  • Outcome improvement unclear: use a bounded pilot or, where feasible, a properly designed controlled comparison. Limited traffic may support exploratory learning without a reliable uplift estimate.
  • Production behaviour unclear: plan staged exposure during implementation, with the required monitoring and recovery evidence. Carry the learning question into validation handover.

A proof of concept, proof of value and MVP describe the purpose or scope of a learning effort; none specifies a complete experimental design. State the actual method, comparator and evidence limits in the record.

Give the prototype an owner and expiry date. Supply relevant design-system components, interaction states, content and accessibility expectations when asking AI to generate it. Review and correct the output before testing; promotion to production follows the applicable architecture, security, testing and operational checks.

Test the real technical limits

For a critical dependency, test the intended integration, identity and data path wherever permitted. Use representative volumes and failure cases for the decision being made. Record mocked components, unavailable access, environmental differences and assumptions that remain untested; an unavailable dependency is an open risk.

Report feasibility as supported under stated conditions, unsupported or inconclusive, with a confidence explanation. Link measurements, versions, test setup and findings to the concept. Use the results to revise scope, quality targets, architecture options, cost ranges or the recommendation.

Reference: [7] GOV.UK alpha guidance includes testing risky assumptions such as integration with existing technology. The reporting format above is this guide’s recommendation.

Generate alternatives from verified findings

After a test, use the reviewed findings to generate different responses to the same need. Keep the original observations and test criteria alongside each proposed change. Compare alternatives by the failure they address, the value assumption they test and the technical work they require.

Include a simpler or non-AI approach where useful. Engineering checks whether the new behaviour remains feasible, and Design checks the complete journey. Select the smallest useful follow-up experiment; more generated variants are useful only when they expose a choice worth testing.

Test complete workflows

For complex administrative workflows, test a realistic task across screens, roles and systems. Include approvals, waiting, missing information, interruption and recovery. Observe whether users can identify their progress, understand the next action and resume safely.

Choose participants to cover relevant user groups, experience levels and access needs. Record gaps and run further targeted tests when those gaps could change the decision. A count of customer conversations alone does not establish adequate evidence.

Test the experience when an agent acts for a user

When the product will be operated by AI agents, test that interaction during discovery. Sumit Sheth calls this agentic user experience (AUX): designing how agents use a product alongside its human experience. Exposing an API alone does not establish a useful journey.

The following are suggested discovery checks for such products. For software that only uses AI during development, continue with the usual user and service journeys.

Suggested checks for a journey carried out by an agent
Part of the journeyWhat to test
Intent and contextWhat to testCan the agent identify the intended task, obtain permitted context and ask for missing information without inventing it?
Permission and controlWhat to testCan the user see the proposed action, set its scope, give any required approval and stop further work?
Action and resultWhat to testCan the agent choose the appropriate operation and distinguish a completed task from a request that was merely accepted?
Failure and recoveryWhat to testWhat happens after a timeout, partial completion, ambiguous instruction or denied access? Check that a retry does not duplicate a consequential action.
Explanation and handbackWhat to testCan the user inspect what changed, correct the result, recover where possible and take over with enough context?

Example · fictional agent journey

For an assistant that submits access requests, test a sandbox journey with missing details, approval refused and a timeout after submission. Observe whether it asks for clarification, respects the refusal and checks request status before retrying. Record task correctness, duplicate requests and the effort needed to take over.

Record the model, tool interface, permissions and test conditions with the prototype version. Repeat variable behaviours and inspect the resulting system state. Use the AI evaluation guidance to plan deeper checks during implementation.

Inspiration: [5] on AUX. The checks and example above are this guide’s recommendations.

Next step: name the uncertainty you most need to resolve. Use the prototype table to choose the simplest experiment that could change the team’s mind.

Source: [3].

Review evidence and decide

Validation is useful only when the method matches the question. Before testing, write down the assumption, choose representative participants or data, set a success threshold and name the decision the result will inform. Feedback then becomes evidence rather than opinion.

Run a repeatable experiment cycle

Product School organises experimentation around a goal, hypothesis, measures, design, execution and learning [9]. Use the following working record for user, business and technical tests; adapt the design to the claim being tested.

  1. Define the decision and outcome. Link the experiment to an opportunity and the investment it will inform. Name the owner, target users or systems and current baseline.
  2. State a falsifiable hypothesis. Specify the change or capability, expected result and reason. Include evidence that would weaken the claim; identify related feasibility assumptions.
  3. Set measures and decision limits. Choose a primary outcome, meaningful improvement or operating threshold, guardrails, learning budget and actions for supported, unsupported or inconclusive findings.
  4. Design and prepare. Choose the method, participants or dataset, comparator, allocation where relevant, versions, environment and dependencies. Agree sample rationale, duration and stopping rule. Link the experiment safety checks and check instrumentation before collecting evidence.
  5. Run and monitor. Record exposures, observations, technical results and deviations. Check data quality and safety guardrails; stop for harm or invalid collection. Preserve the agreed analysis rule rather than ending a test when a favourable result first appears.
  6. Analyse and decide. Compare results with the baseline and decision limits, report uncertainty and limitations, and separate observations from explanations. Record the next action and owner; update the brief, PRD, technical findings and handover record.

For controlled online tests, Microsoft’s experimentation guidance [15] covers success metrics, statistical power, allocation units and data-quality risks. The six-step record above extends the existing discovery checks; it does not prescribe a universal sample count or duration.

Example · fictional experiment

A service desk squad tests whether a draft-response assistant helps staff handle routine access requests. Eight staff complete comparable tasks using the current workflow and a prototype, with the order varied. The team records completion time, correctness, corrections and requests for help.

For this exploratory test, the team agrees to continue only if at least six participants complete the task correctly without help, the median time improves, and no response exposes restricted information. A mixed result triggers another targeted test.

Interpret results within the experiment design

Report observed success separately from stated preference. For controlled tests, review allocation and data quality before interpreting uplift. Report the effect and uncertainty alongside practical value, rather than treating statistical significance as the decision itself. A failed guardrail can outweigh a better primary metric.

Choose duration and sample size for the outcome, expected effect, relevant usage cycles and analysis method. A calendar week or a fixed participant count does not establish adequate evidence. If the available evidence cannot distinguish the options, record an inconclusive result and decide whether a further test is worth its cost.

Test with the people who will use it

The Defence Product Playbook groups fast learning into four habits, which it calls TEST:

  • Trial with real operators: test with the people who will use the product, not project team members standing in for them.
  • Expose the riskiest assumption: build the least you can to test the assumption most likely to sink the product, then discard it.
  • Shorten the loop: measure the time from user feedback to a changed prototype in days. If the loop is slow, fix that first.
  • Turn tests into decisions: end each test by keeping, changing or dropping the idea.

The playbook also gives reference points for pace: a proof of concept in front of real users within three to six months, and a proof of value with real users within a year. It presents these as prompts, not targets. If a team cannot reach them, ask what blocks it: access to users, procurement, funding or the team’s structure.

Fast iteration does not loosen assurance. Track resilience and security as guardrail measures alongside the value measure, and escalate any trade-off that carries real risk to the people authorised to accept it.

End every loop with an explicit decision

Distinguish three decisions. Each needs evidence proportionate to its scope and consequences; success at one does not establish readiness for the next.

Evidence for investigation, implementation and production decisions
DecisionEvidence to review
Worth investigatingA credible problem, obligation or foreseeable risk; the consequence of doing nothing; a material uncertainty; and a bounded, permitted research or experiment plan with an owner and budget.
Worth a bounded implementationEvidence supporting the chosen problem and solution under recorded conditions; critical technical assumptions tested, feasible scope, measurable quality targets, confirmed dependencies, acceptance criteria, expected value, cost and constraints; and owners for remaining uncertainties and risks.
Safe for productionEvidence from the implemented product against applicable release criteria: security, privacy, accessibility, reliability, operational readiness, monitoring and recovery, with residual risks reviewed by the authorised decision makers. Prototype results alone do not establish this.

Review the evidence against the decision rule. When it supports implementation of a bounded scope, record a commitment decision and prepare the handoff. Otherwise choose one of the responses below. Defer when a dependency or timing issue prevents a useful next step; name a review date or reopening trigger. If evidence is inconclusive, record that explicitly and identify the next test within the agreed budget.

Responses when the team is not ready to commit
DecisionUse whenTypical next move
ImproveThe thesis is supported, but execution is underperforming.Tune usability, reliability, performance, cost or operating details.
RedesignThe problem is valid, but the current solution is weak.Explore a materially different solution.
PivotEvidence points to a different user, problem or value.Reframe the thesis and restart discovery.
StopThe thesis, cost, strategic fit or acceptable risk is not supported.Stop investing; keep the learning and any reusable assets.

A decision review can consider six dimensions: problem evidence, solution evidence, strategic fit, cost, risk and how the learning is trending. Agree limits on time, experiments or spending in advance. Stopping a weak thesis early is a successful learning outcome.

Example · feasibility changes the concept

Users complete an access-request prototype successfully. A technical spike finds that the identity service cannot enforce the proposed permissions within the available interface. The team narrows the first scope to drafting requests for human submission, records automated submission as unvalidated, and retests the revised workflow and value.

Keep reviews light and regular

Use focused reviews during each meaningful learning cycle, with broader input when a change affects other teams or shared patterns. A suggested approach is:

  • Focused design review: Product, Design and Engineering examine the prototype, user evidence, accessibility, design-system patterns and feasibility. Record changes and unresolved questions.
  • Cross-team review: invite people who own affected services, domain rules, shared components or controls. Ask for specific feedback on dependencies and inconsistencies. Size participation to the decision; collect input asynchronously where practical.

The decision owner records which feedback changes the proposal and why. A review supplies evidence and advice; formal approval follows the applicable decision authority. At each evidence review, ask:

  1. What uncertainty did we address?
  2. What evidence changed our belief?
  3. What is now the highest-risk assumption?
  4. What decision is justified now that was not justified before?

Check how the concept has changed

Before committing more investment, compare the current proposal with the concept brief. Repeat this check when evidence materially changes the direction. Record:

  • Intent and evidence: changes to the user, problem, outcome or solution, and the findings that explain them.
  • Scope and risk: additions, removals, dependencies and changes to permissions, controls or expected value.
  • Effort and cost: updated estimates from Engineering and other relevant contributors, including ranges, assumptions and uncertainty.
  • Decision: whether the next investment remains justified, who decides and what still needs testing.

Keep justified changes visible in the brief and PRD. Preserve earlier test criteria and results; agree revised criteria before the next experiment.

Keep human approval where the consequences exceed the organisation’s risk tolerance. Examples include material regulatory interpretation, irreversible commitments to users, security exceptions, high-impact automated actions, costly architecture decisions and deployment into sensitive domains. Widen agent autonomy only when permissions, evaluation coverage, monitoring, known failure modes and rollback make the remaining risk acceptable.

Next step: at the end of your next prototype test, record whether to commit to a bounded scope, improve, redesign, pivot or stop. Link the evidence and any remaining uncertainty to that decision.

Source: [1] “Test early, iterate fast”.

4 Complete validation handover

Validation handover is a shared review of what the evidence supports and what implementation still needs to prove. Product, Design and Engineering walk through the same bounded scope with the people planning delivery. Version the package and link each material claim to its research or experiment evidence.

Validation handover package
ArtefactContent to carry forwardReadiness check
Opportunity and decisionContent to carry forwardProblem, users, outcome, baseline, alternatives, selected concept and reasons; the next investment, decision owner and date.Readiness checkThe recommendation follows from the evidence, including conflicting findings and rejected options.
PRD and experienceContent to carry forwardBounded scope, exclusions, stories, acceptance criteria, quality targets and UI artefacts or representative API interactions.Readiness checkThe intended behaviour is testable, including failure, permission, recovery and accessibility cases.
Validation evidenceContent to carry forwardAssumptions, test criteria, method, participants or datasets, versions, results, limitations and evidence links.Readiness checkSupported, unsupported and inconclusive claims are distinct; tests cover the highest-risk business and technical assumptions.
Technical findingsContent to carry forwardSystem and data-flow context, approach options, spike results, dependency confirmations, initial architecture decisions and build/run cost ranges.Readiness checkEngineering can explain why the bounded scope appears feasible and which conditions limit that conclusion.
Remaining uncertaintyContent to carry forwardRisk or unknown, potential impact, owner, next check, time or cost bound, and trigger to reconsider scope or stop.Readiness checkBlocking unknowns return to discovery. Any accepted uncertainty has an explicit resolution and escalation route.
Delivery and measurementContent to carry forwardThe first useful slice, outcome and guardrail measures, telemetry and evaluation needs, and production evidence still required.Readiness checkThe delivery team can plan the TRD and tasks, collect missing evidence and identify when to reopen discovery.

For material AI-assisted findings, retain the reviewed source extract, relevant model or tool version, task instructions, reviewer and decision link, with access appropriate to the data. Keep generated scenarios and discarded interpretations identifiable. Delivery should be able to trace a requirement to evidence without mistaking a model’s inference for a user finding.

Make the next commitment explicit

The review should distinguish a request for more investigation from a commitment to bounded implementation. The authorised decision owner records the investment and scope decision, informed by Product, Design, Engineering and relevant specialists. Review participation does not create approval authority.

  • Product and Design: explain the need, expected value, tested experience, evidence limits and acceptance criteria.
  • Engineering and Operations: explain the technical evidence, dependencies, delivery assumptions, operating constraints and unresolved feasibility risks.
  • Delivery contributors: walk the first slice, identify contradictions and confirm that the package is usable for planning. Record actions and owners in the shared decision record.

When an unknown could invalidate the core concept, test it or narrow the scope before committing to delivery that depends on it. Other uncertainty can continue into a bounded implementation when its impact, owner, resolution plan and decision limits are explicit and accepted by the relevant authority. A completed PRD alone does not establish readiness.

Include the experiment safety record and disposition of prototype code, data and credentials. For an agentic experience, carry forward tested action boundaries, approval points, failure and recovery cases and evaluation results. Prototype success supports only the recorded conditions; production release needs the applicable implementation and release evidence.

Keep discovery connected to delivery

Continue Product, Design and Engineering collaboration as the TRD, tasks and implemented behaviour develop. Reopen the relevant discovery question if a dependency fails, expected value weakens, scope changes materially, or performance and operating cost cannot meet the agreed limits. Route bounded implementation defects to delivery; retain the decision history when the product direction changes.

Use the shared handoff package and readiness checks as the connection between loops. Keep evidence and decisions accessible in the same product context, with access appropriate to the data.

Continue to implementation readiness: use the technical findings to develop the TRD and verifiable tasks.

Keep product intent connected

Product intent is the reasoning behind a product: why it exists, what it does, and the limits it works within. In many teams that reasoning is scattered across separate tools for evidence, requirements, design, architecture, policies and success measures. Missing or contradictory context can lead agents to make unsupported assumptions. Keep the sources, decisions and unresolved questions accessible together.

Trace outcomes into required behaviour and enabling architecture. Policies constrain all three, and evaluation checks all three. Keep these reasons explicit:

  • a product behaviour exists because it supports a user and business outcome;
  • an architecture choice exists because it enables required behaviour under known constraints;
  • a policy control exists because it addresses a defined risk; and
  • an evaluation shows whether the intended behaviour and constraints are met.

Keep product intent versioned, owned, accessible and auditable. Where practical, make the most valuable parts machine-readable: API descriptions, schemas, policy rules, acceptance tests and evaluation datasets can be checked automatically, not only read.

Make asynchronous decisions traceable

Attach feedback to a specific version of the brief, prototype or PRD. State the question, response deadline and decision owner. Keep one linked decision record with the date, options considered, evidence, rationale, actions and superseded decisions.

Use AI to draft a register of disputed assumptions from permitted discussion notes. Ask contributors to confirm the interpretation. Distinguish a missing fact from an investment, policy or ownership decision: more research cannot settle every disagreement. Record the evidence needed or authorised decision owner, rather than treating apparent consensus as validation. Use recordings only where permitted, with agreed access and retention.

Treat the specification as a living document

In AI-assisted development, the specification is both an instruction for generating work and a basis for checking it. GitHub’s Spec Kit describes a common pattern that moves from a specification to a technical plan, then to tasks and implementation. During discovery, the specification develops alongside the evidence:

  1. Product intent is drafted as a PRD.
  2. User experiments and technical spikes test its riskiest assumptions.
  3. The evidence revises the PRD, quality targets and technical options.
  4. When evidence supports a bounded implementation, the team versions the PRD and linked artefacts for handover.

A useful specification is explicit enough to expose ambiguity, testable through examples, acceptance tests or evaluations, versioned and linked to outcomes, clear about constraints, permissions, non-functional requirements, edge cases and exclusions, and open to revision when evidence changes the intent.

Balance the level of detail. Too little forces agents to guess critical intent; too much creates false certainty. Increase precision as uncertainty is retired. Read about spec-driven development.

Next step: pick one planned behaviour in your PRD. Trace it up to the user outcome it serves and down to the test or evaluation that will show it works; fill any missing link.

Source: [4].

Measure learning and outcomes, not activity

Faster generation creates value only when the team can turn output into evidence, and evidence into better decisions. Start collecting evidence at the prototype stage instead of waiting for production. The cycle is: build, observe, evaluate, learn, update the product intent, and build again.

Draw on several kinds of evidence

  • User evidence: interviews, usability studies, support cases and co-creation sessions.
  • Behavioural evidence: product analytics, controlled experiments, workflow completion and adoption.
  • Operational evidence: telemetry, reliability, latency, incidents, model traces and recovery.
  • Evaluation evidence: offline datasets, automated tests, agent evaluations, policy checks and calibrated model-based judges.
  • Cost evidence: experiment cost, delivery effort, inference cost and the human attention consumed.

Check whether AI assistance improves the research task itself. For a sample reviewed by a researcher, record missed findings, unsupported claims, lost context and time spent checking or correcting outputs. Compare with the current method before increasing automation. Faster drafting is useful when the total effort falls without losing material evidence. Read how to evaluate AI behaviour and check model-based judgements.

Link each result to its research notes, dataset or test run. Keep participant information in the appropriate controlled location and summarise only what the decision needs. When evidence conflicts, record the conflict rather than averaging it into a reassuring conclusion.

Product, Design and Engineering should review feedback from use together. If evidence challenges the user need or intended behaviour, reopen discovery; if it reveals a bounded implementation defect, route it to delivery. Change the product intent through a recorded decision; feedback does not automatically authorise model retraining or broader agent permissions.

Define success before building

Features shipped, prototypes generated, prompts submitted and lines of AI-generated code measure activity. They do not show user impact or business value. Define measures at each of these layers:

Suggested measurement layers; set local measures and thresholds before testing
LayerWhat it answers
User outcomeDid the user achieve the outcome that makes the product worthwhile?
Business outcomeDid the product create the intended value for the organisation?
Product behaviourDid users adopt the behaviour that should drive the outcome?
Leading indicatorsAre early signals moving in the expected direction?
Learning speed and costHow quickly and affordably did a hypothesis become credible evidence and a decision?
GuardrailsDid quality, safety, reliability, cost, privacy and fairness stay within tolerance?

Choose a value measure to steer by

The Defence Product Playbook describes a ladder of four kinds of measure. Use it to connect effort and early signals to value and longer-term outcomes. The adaptation below distinguishes resource inputs from usage and operational measures; a measure’s role depends on the product and its theory of change.

The metric ladder, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
RungWhat it shows
1. Input measureResources invested, such as team effort, funding or compute
2. Leading indicatorAn early behaviour change that supports part of the theory of change
3. Value measureThe intended outcome of solving the problem; the measure the team steers by
4. Outcome measureThe effect the organisation ultimately seeks; often slower to change than measures used to guide weekly work

Higher rungs aim to measure effects closer to the intended value, but confidence still depends on evidence quality and the causal link between measures. The playbook recommends one value measure per problem that can move at least twice a year. Explain how improving it contributes to the outcome above it, and test that relationship.

Uptime is an operational reliability measure. Depending on the product, it may be a guardrail, a service outcome or a direct contributor to mission value. Usage can be a leading indicator when evidence links it to the intended outcome. Neither is naturally a resource input, and neither alone demonstrates that the problem is being solved.

Challenge a candidate measure if it can improve without improving the intended outcome, or if its causal link is untested. Retain system measures where they reveal a relevant operating constraint or outcome. Self-reported satisfaction, perceived effort and trust can also be meaningful outcomes; triangulate them with behavioural and operational evidence, and record sampling and response biases. Check measures against SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Weigh value against cost. The playbook’s value-cost ratio divides the outcome delivered by annual cost and tracks its year-on-year change. Treat this as an efficiency measure with explicit outcome units, cost scope and measurement period. It is not automatically financial return on investment (ROI); financial ROI needs justified monetary benefits and costs. Compare ratios only when outcome units and cost boundaries are comparable, or when a defensible common valuation explains the comparison.

When measured value plateaus, investigate whether the product is sustaining an essential outcome or meeting an obligation before shifting investment. Maintenance may preserve mission value, supportability and risk controls even when the headline measure no longer rises.

Measures worth considering include:

  • Time to validated learning: elapsed time from an explicit hypothesis to credible evidence and a decision.
  • Cost per experiment: the cost of producing credible learning, including compute and human review.
  • Evidence quality and human attention: source accuracy, omitted or unsupported findings, review and correction effort, and whether assistance leaves more time for direct user contact and difficult decisions.
  • Product guardrails: task success, correction and escalation rates, model errors, latency, reliability, cost, privacy and safety incidents, fairness where material, and user trust.

Next step: for your next experiment, write the hypothesis, its start date and the success threshold. Record the date of the resulting decision to measure time to validated learning.

Source: [1] “Define the problem, measure the value”.

Common discovery gaps and controls

Failure patterns to check at each evidence review
GapConsequenceWorking control
Starting from a requested featureConsequenceThe team refines a solution without showing that it addresses the underlying need.Working controlTrace the request to research and compare different concepts, including non-software options.
Deferring feasibility to implementationConsequenceData, integration or operating limits invalidate the concept after commitment.Working controlInclude Engineering from research onwards and test the critical technical path before dependent scope is committed.
Treating a demo as validationConsequencePolish or a successful mock conceals weak value evidence and unavailable dependencies.Working controlSeparate user, business and technical claims; link each to a suitable experiment and its limits.
Research without a decisionConsequenceThe team collects information without reducing a material uncertainty.Working controlName the next decision, owner, learning budget and evidence threshold before the work starts.
A document-only handoverConsequenceDelivery inherits unexplained choices, hidden risks and requirements disconnected from evidence.Working controlWalk the bounded scope together and carry evidence, technical findings and owned unknowns into planning.
